subject: Digital Construction & RC
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Build the Job Before You Get to the Job
subHeading: How digital construction can help reinforced concrete contractors review the work, identify issues and prepare for site.
abstract: Discover how independent drawing reviews, 3D modelling and constructability checks can help RC contractors identify questions early, check materials and interfaces, communicate with clients, support site teams and build a portfolio of completed projects.
body:
## The idea

Before work starts on site, an RC contractor has an opportunity to understand the job in three dimensions rather than relying on drawings alone.

By having the drawings independently reviewed and the concrete package modelled in 3D, contractors can identify questions, review how the work fits together and develop a clearer picture of what they intend to construct.

The principle is simple: **build the job before you get to the job.**

## 01 — Get an independent review of the drawings

An outside review provides another set of eyes on the construction package.

It creates an opportunity to identify unclear information, inconsistencies and areas that need further clarification before the contractor commits resources to the work.

The aim is to help the contractor understand the package and identify the questions that need answering.

## 02 — Build the job in 3D before arriving on site

A 3D model turns the information contained in the drawings into a visual representation of the proposed concrete works.

Foundations, columns, beams, slabs and reinforcement can be brought together in one model, helping the contractor see how the different elements relate to one another.

Instead of trying to picture the entire job from separate 2D views, the team has another way to understand what it is being asked to build.

## 03 — Identify issues and prepare RFIs

The model and drawing review can help highlight areas where information is missing, unclear or requires confirmation.

These observations can be recorded and used to prepare requests for information (RFIs) for the relevant design team.

Raising questions early gives the project team more opportunity to resolve them before they affect construction on site.

## 04 — Check materials, fit and constructability

A digital review provides an opportunity to consider whether the proposed work fits together and can be constructed as intended.

Are the materials and quantities consistent with the drawings? Do the different elements fit together? Is there enough space or any unforseen clashes? Are there any areas that need further investigation before construction begins?

These checks help the contractor develop a clearer understanding of the package and identify potential problems while there is still time to address them.

## 05 — Show the client what you intend to build

A 3D model provides a visual reference that can be shared with the client and project team before construction starts.

It helps communicate the intended outcome, making it easier to discuss the scope of work, clarify expectations and agree on the specification.

Everyone has an opportunity to review the proposed work and raise questions before the contractor starts building.

## 06 — Give the site team another reference

Construction drawings remain essential, but some details can be difficult to visualise from 2D views alone.

A 3D model provides an additional reference that site managers and fixing teams can consult when reviewing complex or unclear areas of the package.

It helps the team understand how the different elements are intended to come together, supporting communication between the office and the people carrying out the work.

The model complements approved construction information; it does not replace it.

## 07 — Build a portfolio of completed projects

The value of the model does not have to end when the concrete work is complete.

With the appropriate permissions, models and project views can be retained as evidence of the contractor's work and used in future tenders, client presentations and marketing.

A digital portfolio gives prospective clients a visual way to understand the contractor's capabilities and the type of projects they deliver.

## Build the job before you get to the job

An independent drawing review and 3D model give RC contractors another way to understand their construction package before work begins.

From identifying questions and checking how the work fits together to agreeing on the intended outcome with the client and supporting the site team, digital construction can help bring important conversations forward.

It also leaves the contractor with a reusable digital record of the project.

The aim isn't to promise a problem-free project. It's to identify what can be checked, clarified and agreed before the team arrives on site.

**Review it. Model it. Resolve the questions. Then get to site with a clearer picture of the job.**

Hammond BIM Tech provides BIM modelling, independent drawing review support, constructability reviews and model-based quantity take-offs for construction teams.

subject: Digital Construction & Software
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Should Construction Hire Software Engineers?
subHeading: Why construction companies might need to start hiring software engineers instead of solving every digital problem by buying another piece of software.
abstract: Construction companies are increasingly dependent on software, but does every digital problem need another commercial platform? Explore the case for bringing software engineers into construction teams to build tools, connect systems and develop technology around the way the business actually works.
body:
## The idea

Construction has become increasingly dependent on software.

Design teams use Revit, Civil 3D and Tekla. Contractors use estimating systems, planning software, CDEs and site-management platforms. Clients expect structured information, digital models and increasingly sophisticated reporting.

There is nothing wrong with using specialist software. In many cases, it is exactly the right tool for the job.

But there is another question worth asking: why does construction tend to buy software to solve its problems rather than hiring people who can build the solutions themselves?

## 01 — Buy software or build capability?

When a construction company identifies a problem, the usual response is often to look for software that already solves it.

Perhaps another platform is purchased. Perhaps consultants are brought in to implement it. Perhaps the project team is trained to follow a new workflow.

But what if the company hired a software engineer instead?

The engineer could understand the problem, investigate the existing systems and build a solution specifically around the way that company works.

It might be a small internal application, an API connecting two systems, an automated report, a database or simply a script that removes a repetitive task.

The difference is important: the company hasn't just bought another product. It has gained a technical capability.

## 02 — Construction professionals already have enough jobs

Consider a site manager.

They are already responsible for coordinating subcontractors, managing programme, dealing with safety, checking quality, solving problems and keeping the project moving.

Now introduce another digital platform and ask them to change the way they work around it.

They have to learn the software, follow the workflow and make sure their team uses it correctly.

But becoming good at construction and becoming good at software are different skills.

Why should a site manager have to become a software expert simply because their company wants to improve the way information is managed?

Perhaps the answer is to have someone whose job is specifically to solve that problem.

## 03 — Put technical people alongside construction teams

Imagine a contractor with a small internal team of software engineers, data specialists and BIM professionals.

Their role isn't to replace the construction professionals or tell them how to run a project.

Their role is to understand how the business already works and then improve the technology supporting it.

A project manager might explain that producing a particular report takes several hours every week.

A quantity surveyor might explain that information has to be copied manually between different systems.

A site manager might explain that the information available in the office isn't presented in a useful way on site.

These are construction problems.

But the solution may be a software problem.

Having people who understand software inside the organisation means those problems can be investigated and potentially solved rather than simply accepted as part of the job.

## 04 — This doesn't mean replacing commercial software

The argument isn't that construction companies should build everything themselves.

Revit is an incredibly powerful design platform. Tekla provides highly specialised modelling capabilities. Civil 3D serves a specific engineering purpose. Commercial CDEs can provide useful collaboration and information-management functions.

Building replacements for all of these would make little sense for most companies.

The more interesting question is what happens around them.

A contractor can use the best commercial software available while still having its own people build the connections, automations and tools that make those systems work better for the business.

Use the software where it makes sense. Build what is specific to your business.

## 05 — Software engineers could work on the gaps

Commercial software has to be designed for a large number of customers.

That means it needs to be flexible enough to work for many different companies and industries.

A construction company, however, has its own processes, standards and requirements.

There will always be problems that are too specific for a software vendor to solve perfectly.

This is where internal software development becomes interesting.

A company could build a tool that connects its BIM models to its own databases. It could automate quantity extraction, create project-specific dashboards, connect systems through APIs or develop internal QA tools.

The goal isn't to compete with the major software companies.

It is to fill the gaps between their products and the way the construction company actually works.

## 06 — Look at what other industries do

This idea isn't particularly unusual outside construction.

Manufacturing companies employ software engineers, automation specialists, data analysts and systems engineers alongside their production and engineering teams.

Healthcare organisations have technical teams working alongside doctors, nurses and administrators.

Financial companies employ enormous software engineering teams because technology is part of how the business operates.

In these industries, software isn't simply something the organisation buys.

Software is part of the organisation's capability.

Construction has traditionally been much more comfortable treating software as an external product.

Perhaps that needs to change.

## 07 — From software users to software capability

There is a difference between having lots of software and having the ability to use technology effectively.

A company can spend millions on licences and still have inefficient processes, disconnected systems and people manually moving information between applications.

Hiring software engineers doesn't automatically solve those problems either.

The important part is putting technical people close enough to the construction business to understand what actually needs improving.

The construction team understands the work.

The software team understands how to turn problems into technical solutions.

The two need to work together.

## Should construction hire software engineers?

The answer probably isn't to stop buying software.

Construction will always need specialist commercial applications, and many of them are exceptionally difficult to replace.

The question is whether buying software should be the default answer to every digital problem.

Perhaps a mature construction company should have both:

Specialist software for specialist problems.

Software engineers for company-specific problems.

That creates a different kind of digital capability.

Instead of asking every construction professional to adapt themselves to another piece of software, the company has people whose job is to make technology work around the business.

The aim isn't to build everything yourself.

It's to know what is worth buying, what is worth building and where the two need to connect.

Maybe construction's next digital investment shouldn't always be another software licence. Maybe sometimes it should be the person who can build what the software doesn't.

Hammond BIM Tech explores BIM, construction technology, data and digital workflows, with a focus on practical ways technology can improve how construction projects are designed, built and managed.
